notes.title: Number Systems and Data Representation
notes.body:
Computers store everything in binary, so knowing how integers, negative numbers, characters and real numbers are encoded explains overflow, precision and many classic bugs.

### Bases
| Base | Digits | Example (decimal 45) |
|---|---|---|
| Binary (2) | 0–1 | `101101` |
| Octal (8) | 0–7 | `55` |
| Decimal (10) | 0–9 | `45` |
| Hexadecimal (16) | 0–9, A–F | `2D` |

One hex digit is exactly 4 bits, which is why memory addresses and colours are written in hex.

### Signed integers
| Scheme | −5 in 8 bits | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Sign-magnitude | `10000101` | Two zeros (+0 and −0) |
| One's complement | `11111010` | Flip all bits; still two zeros |
| **Two's complement** | `11111011` | Flip the bits and add 1; one zero; used by all modern CPUs |

An n-bit two's complement integer ranges from **−2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1**. For 8 bits that's −128 to 127. Adding 1 to 127 **overflows** to −128.

### Floating point (IEEE 754)
A single-precision float (32 bits) has 1 **sign** bit, 8 **exponent** bits (bias 127) and 23 **mantissa** (fraction) bits.
Value = (−1)^sign × 1.mantissa × 2^(exponent − 127)

Double precision uses 64 bits (1 + 11 + 52).

**Why `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3`:** 0.1 has no exact binary representation (just as 1/3 has no exact decimal one), so rounding errors appear. Use decimal types or integers (e.g. paise or cents) for money.

Special values: ±0, ±∞, **NaN** (`NaN != NaN`), and denormals for numbers very close to zero.

### Characters
- **ASCII:** 7 bits, 128 characters.
- **Unicode:** code points for every script. **UTF-8** encodes them in 1–4 bytes and is backward-compatible with ASCII.

### Interview questions
**Q: How do you check whether n is a power of two?**
`n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0`. A power of two has exactly one bit set, and subtracting 1 flips that bit and every bit below it.

notes.title: Basic Computer Organization: CPU, ALU, Registers and Buses
notes.body:
A computer's core components (CPU, memory and I/O) are connected by buses, and inside the CPU the control unit, ALU and registers work together to execute instructions.

### The von Neumann architecture
- A single memory holds **both instructions and data**.
- The CPU fetches instructions from memory and executes them one after another.
- **Von Neumann bottleneck:** the shared path between CPU and memory limits throughput. Caches and pipelining exist largely to work around it.

**Harvard architecture:** separate instruction and data memories and paths. It's used in microcontrollers and, effectively, in the split L1 instruction and data caches of modern CPUs.

### Inside the CPU
- **ALU (arithmetic logic unit):** add, subtract, AND, OR, shifts and comparisons. It sets **flags** (zero, carry, overflow, sign).
- **Control unit:** decodes instructions and generates control signals.
- **Registers:** the fastest storage.

| Register | Role |
|---|---|
| PC (program counter) | Address of the next instruction |
| IR (instruction register) | The instruction currently executing |
| MAR (memory address register) | Address to read or write |
| MDR / MBR (memory data register) | Data being transferred |
| Accumulator / general purpose | Operands and results |
| SP (stack pointer) | Top of the stack |
| Status / flags register | Condition codes |

### Buses
- **Address bus:** carries addresses; one-way (CPU → memory). Its width sets how much memory can be addressed (32 bits = 4 GB).
- **Data bus:** carries data; two-way. Its width affects how much moves per transfer.
- **Control bus:** read/write signals, interrupts, clock.

### Performance basics
**CPU time = instruction count × CPI × clock period**, where CPI is cycles per instruction. You can speed a program up by running fewer instructions (a better algorithm or compiler), lowering CPI (pipelining, caching), or raising the clock speed.

### Interview questions
**Q: Why can a 32-bit system address only 4 GB?**
A 32-bit address can represent 2³² distinct byte addresses, which is 4 GiB. PAE and 64-bit addressing remove this limit.

notes.title: Instruction Set Architecture: CISC vs RISC
notes.body:
The instruction set architecture (ISA) is the contract between hardware and software: the instructions, registers, data types and addressing modes a CPU exposes.

### Instruction formats
An instruction encodes an **opcode** (what to do) and **operands** (what to use).
- **Three-address:** `ADD R1, R2, R3` (R1 = R2 + R3)
- **Two-address:** `ADD R1, R2` (R1 = R1 + R2)
- **One-address:** uses an accumulator: `ADD X`
- **Zero-address:** stack machines: `ADD` (pops two values, pushes the sum)

### Instruction types
Data transfer (`LOAD`, `STORE`, `MOV`), arithmetic and logic (`ADD`, `AND`, `SHL`), control flow (`JMP`, `BEQ`, `CALL`, `RET`) and system instructions (`SYSCALL`, `HALT`).

### CISC vs RISC
| | CISC | RISC |
|---|---|---|
| Instructions | Many, complex, variable length | Few, simple, fixed length |
| Memory access | Many instructions can touch memory | Only LOAD/STORE touch memory (load-store architecture) |
| Cycles per instruction | Many | About 1 (pipeline-friendly) |
| Registers | Fewer | Many |
| Code size | Smaller | Larger |
| Decoding | Complex (often microcoded) | Simple, hardwired |
| Examples | x86, x86-64 | ARM, RISC-V, MIPS |

### The modern reality
x86 CPUs decode CISC instructions into internal RISC-like **micro-operations** and execute those on a RISC-style core. Meanwhile ARM has gained more complex instructions. The difference is now mainly about **ISA design and power efficiency**. Apple's M-series and most phones run ARM.

### Interview questions
**Q: Why is RISC easier to pipeline?**
Fixed-length, simple instructions take similar time per stage and decode quickly, so the pipeline stays full with few stalls.

notes.title: Addressing Modes
notes.body:
Addressing modes define how an instruction specifies where its operand is: in the instruction itself, in a register, or somewhere in memory computed from registers and constants.

### The common modes
| Mode | Example | Operand is | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Immediate | `MOV R1, #5` | The constant 5 | Constants |
| Register | `ADD R1, R2` | The contents of R2 | Fast temporaries |
| Direct (absolute) | `LOAD R1, 1000` | Memory[1000] | Global variables |
| Indirect | `LOAD R1, (1000)` | Memory[Memory[1000]] | Pointers |
| Register indirect | `LOAD R1, (R2)` | Memory[R2] | Pointer dereference |
| Indexed / displacement | `LOAD R1, 8(R2)` | Memory[R2 + 8] | Arrays, struct fields, stack frames |
| Base + index | `LOAD R1, (R2 + R3)` | Memory[R2 + R3] | Two-dimensional arrays |
| PC-relative | `BEQ +12` | PC + 12 | Branches; position-independent code |
| Auto-increment / decrement | `LOAD R1, (R2)+` | Memory[R2], then R2 += size | Walking arrays, stacks |

### Effective address
The **effective address (EA)** is the final memory address an instruction uses. In indexed mode, EA = base register + displacement.

### Mapping to high-level code
```c
int x = 5;            // immediate
int y = arr[i];       // indexed (base = arr, index = i * 4)
int z = *p;           // register indirect
s.field = 1;          // displacement (base = &s, offset of field)
if (a == b) goto L;   // PC-relative branch
```

### Trade-offs
More addressing modes mean shorter programs (CISC), but more complex decoding and slower pipelines. RISC keeps a few simple modes, usually register, immediate and displacement.

### Interview questions
**Q: Which addressing mode makes code position-independent?**
PC-relative addressing. Targets are offsets from the current instruction, so the code works wherever it's loaded in memory (shared libraries, ASLR).

notes.title: Instruction Cycle and the Control Unit
notes.body:
Every instruction goes through a fetch-decode-execute cycle, coordinated by the control unit, which can be built from fixed logic (hardwired) or from stored microcode (microprogrammed).

### The instruction cycle
1. **Fetch:** MAR ← PC; MDR ← Memory[MAR]; IR ← MDR; PC ← PC + instruction size.
2. **Decode:** the control unit interprets the opcode and identifies the operands.
3. **Operand fetch:** compute the effective address and read the operands.
4. **Execute:** the ALU performs the operation, or a branch updates the PC.
5. **Write back:** store the result in a register or memory.
6. **Interrupt check:** if an interrupt is pending, save the context and jump to its handler.

### Micro-operations
Each step consists of tiny register-transfer operations, e.g. `T1: MAR ← PC`, `T2: MDR ← M[MAR], PC ← PC + 1`, `T3: IR ← MDR`.

### Hardwired vs microprogrammed control
| | Hardwired | Microprogrammed |
|---|---|---|
| Built from | Fixed logic circuits (gates, decoders, flip-flops) | Microinstructions stored in a control memory |
| Speed | Faster | Slower (fetches microinstructions) |
| Flexibility | Hard to change | Easy to modify or extend (update the microcode) |
| Suits | RISC | CISC (complex instructions) |

Modern x86 CPUs use hardwired decoding for common instructions and microcode for rare, complex ones. Microcode updates are even used to patch CPU bugs and security issues.

### Interrupts in the cycle
At the end of each instruction cycle the CPU checks for pending interrupts. This keeps the current instruction atomic and the program state well defined when control passes to the handler.

### Interview questions
**Q: Why is the PC incremented during fetch, not after execution?**
So that it already points to the next sequential instruction. Branches then simply overwrite it during execute.

notes.title: Pipelining and Hazards
notes.body:
Pipelining overlaps the stages of several instructions, like an assembly line, so the CPU completes about one instruction per cycle even though each instruction takes several cycles.

### The classic 5-stage RISC pipeline
**IF** (fetch) → **ID** (decode and register read) → **EX** (execute) → **MEM** (memory access) → **WB** (write back)

| Cycle | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| I1 | IF | ID | EX | MEM | WB | |
| I2 | | IF | ID | EX | MEM | WB |
| I3 | | | IF | ID | EX | MEM |

### Speedup
For n instructions on a k-stage pipeline:
- Non-pipelined: n × k cycles
- Pipelined: k + (n − 1) cycles
- Ideal speedup approaches **k** as n grows large.

### Hazards
| Hazard | Cause | Solutions |
|---|---|---|
| **Structural** | Two instructions need the same hardware at once | Duplicate resources (separate instruction and data caches) |
| **Data** | An instruction needs a result that isn't ready yet | **Forwarding (bypassing)**, stalls, compiler scheduling |
| **Control** | The next instruction depends on a branch outcome | Branch prediction, delayed branches, flushing |

### Data hazard types
- **RAW (read after write):** a true dependency, and the common one.
- **WAR (write after read)** and **WAW (write after write):** name dependencies; they matter in out-of-order CPUs and are removed by **register renaming**.

### Example: load-use hazard
```
LW  R1, 0(R2)
ADD R3, R1, R4    // needs R1 before the load has finished
```
Even with forwarding, one stall cycle is needed, because the data arrives only after the MEM stage. Compilers reorder independent instructions to fill this slot.

### Beyond the basic pipeline
**Superscalar** CPUs issue several instructions per cycle; **out-of-order execution** runs instructions as soon as their operands are ready; **deep pipelines** allow higher clock speeds but pay more on each misprediction.

### Interview questions
**Q: Does pipelining reduce the time to execute a single instruction?**
No. It increases **throughput**, not latency. A single instruction can even take slightly longer because of pipeline register overhead.

notes.title: Branch Prediction and Speculative Execution
notes.body:
Branch prediction guesses which way a conditional jump will go, so the pipeline keeps fetching useful instructions instead of stalling until the branch resolves.

### Why it's needed
In a 15–20 stage pipeline, waiting for each branch to resolve would waste many cycles. Roughly 1 in 5 instructions is a branch.

### Static prediction
- Always predict "not taken", or "taken".
- **Backward taken, forward not taken (BTFN):** loops jump backwards and are usually taken.

### Dynamic prediction
- **1-bit predictor:** remembers the last outcome. A loop mispredicts twice per run (on exit and on re-entry).
- **2-bit saturating counter:** states strongly/weakly taken and not taken. It needs two wrong guesses in a row to flip, so it handles loops well.
- **Correlating / two-level predictors:** use the history of recent branches.
- **TAGE and perceptron predictors:** modern CPUs reach over 95% accuracy.

### Branch target buffer (BTB)
Caches the *target address* of recently taken branches, so the fetch stage knows *where* to go, not just *whether* to jump.

### Speculative execution
The CPU executes instructions down the predicted path before knowing whether the prediction was right.
- **Correct:** the results commit; no time lost.
- **Wrong:** the pipeline is flushed and work restarts on the correct path, costing about 15–20 cycles.

**Spectre and Meltdown (2018)** showed that even discarded speculative work leaves traces in the cache that attackers can measure, which led to major OS and microcode mitigations.

### Writing prediction-friendly code
```c
// Unpredictable branch on random data: slow
for (i = 0; i < n; i++) if (data[i] >= 128) sum += data[i];
```
Sorting `data` first makes the branch predictable and often runs several times faster: the famous Stack Overflow question. Branchless code (conditional moves, arithmetic masks) also helps.

### Interview questions
**Q: Why does a 2-bit predictor beat a 1-bit predictor for loops?**
At loop exit a 1-bit predictor flips to "not taken" and then mispredicts again when the loop starts next time. A 2-bit counter tolerates one exception without flipping its prediction.

notes.title: The Memory Hierarchy
notes.body:
The memory hierarchy layers small, fast, expensive storage over large, slow, cheap storage, and relies on locality so that most accesses hit the fast levels.

### Typical levels (approximate)
| Level | Size | Latency | Managed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registers | < 1 KB | ~0.3 ns (1 cycle) | Compiler |
| L1 cache | 32–64 KB per core | ~1 ns (4 cycles) | Hardware |
| L2 cache | 256 KB–2 MB per core | ~3–5 ns | Hardware |
| L3 cache | 8–64 MB shared | ~10–20 ns | Hardware |
| Main memory (DRAM) | 8–128 GB | ~60–100 ns | OS |
| SSD | 0.5–4 TB | ~20–100 µs | OS / file system |
| HDD | Several TB | ~5–10 ms | OS / file system |

A main-memory access costs about **100–300 CPU cycles**. Cache efficiency often dominates real-world performance.

### Locality of reference
- **Temporal locality:** recently used data is likely to be used again soon (loop variables).
- **Spatial locality:** nearby addresses are likely to be used soon (array traversal).

Caches exploit both: they keep recent data and fetch whole **cache lines** (usually 64 bytes).

### Average memory access time (AMAT)
**AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty**
Example: L1 hit 1 ns, miss rate 5%, miss penalty 100 ns, so AMAT = 1 + 0.05 × 100 = **6 ns**.

### SRAM vs DRAM
| | SRAM | DRAM |
|---|---|---|
| Cell | 6 transistors | 1 transistor + 1 capacitor |
| Speed | Fast | Slower |
| Refresh | Not needed | Needed (capacitors leak) |
| Cost and density | Expensive, low density | Cheap, high density |
| Used for | Caches | Main memory |

### Interview questions
**Q: Why is iterating over a 2D array row by row faster than column by column in C?**
C stores arrays in row-major order. Row-wise traversal walks consecutive addresses, using each 64-byte cache line fully. Column-wise traversal jumps a whole row each step, missing the cache constantly.

notes.title: Cache Memory and Mapping
notes.body:
A cache is a small, fast memory that holds copies of recently used blocks of main memory; its mapping, replacement and write policies decide where data goes and what is evicted.

### Address breakdown
A memory address is split into **tag | index | block offset**.
- **Offset:** the byte within the cache line (64-byte lines need 6 bits).
- **Index:** which set the line maps to.
- **Tag:** identifies which memory block is currently stored there.

### Mapping techniques
| Mapping | A block can go | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| Direct-mapped | Exactly one line | Simple, fast lookup | Conflict misses |
| Fully associative | Any line | Fewest conflict misses | Costly parallel tag comparison |
| N-way set-associative | Any of N lines in one set | Good balance (used in practice) | Moderate complexity |

### Worked example
32 KB cache, 64-byte lines, 8-way set-associative, 32-bit addresses:
- Lines = 32 KB / 64 B = 512; sets = 512 / 8 = 64.
- Offset = 6 bits, index = log₂ 64 = 6 bits, tag = 32 − 12 = **20 bits**.

### The three Cs of misses
- **Compulsory:** the first access to a block (cold miss).
- **Capacity:** the working set is larger than the cache.
- **Conflict:** too many blocks map to the same set.

### Replacement policies
LRU (or pseudo-LRU in hardware), FIFO, random.

### Write policies
| Policy | On a write hit | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Write-through | Write to the cache **and** memory | Simple and consistent; more memory traffic (needs write buffers) |
| Write-back | Write to the cache only; mark the line **dirty**; write to memory on eviction | Less traffic; more complex |

On a write **miss**: **write-allocate** (load the line, then write; usually paired with write-back) or **no-write-allocate** (write straight to memory; usually paired with write-through).

### Interview questions
**Q: Why not make L1 bigger to avoid misses?**
A larger cache is slower to access (longer wires, more ways to compare). L1 must respond in about 4 cycles, so it stays small, and bigger, slower levels sit behind it.

notes.title: Cache Coherence and False Sharing
notes.body:
In multi-core CPUs each core has its own cache, so the hardware must keep copies of shared data consistent (coherence); false sharing is the performance trap this creates.

### The coherence problem
Core 0 and core 1 both cache variable `x`. If core 0 writes `x`, core 1's copy is stale. Coherence protocols make sure every core eventually sees the latest value of each memory location.

### MESI protocol
Each cache line is in one of four states:
| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **M**odified | Only this cache has it, and it's dirty |
| **E**xclusive | Only this cache has it, and it's clean |
| **S**hared | Several caches have clean copies |
| **I**nvalid | Not valid in this cache |

Writing to a Shared line **invalidates** other cores' copies first. Variants: **MOESI** (AMD) and **MESIF** (Intel).

### Snooping vs directory protocols
- **Snooping:** caches watch a shared bus for other cores' operations. Simple, but doesn't scale to many cores.
- **Directory-based:** a directory tracks which caches hold each line. Scales better.

### False sharing
Two threads update **different variables** that happen to sit on the **same 64-byte cache line**. Each write invalidates the other core's copy, so the line bounces between cores ("cache-line ping-pong"), even though no data is logically shared.

```java
class Counters {
    volatile long a;   // thread 1 writes
    volatile long b;   // thread 2 writes; same cache line, so false sharing
}
```
**Fixes:** pad or align hot variables to separate lines (Java's `@Contended`, C++ `alignas(64)`, or padding fields), or have each thread accumulate locally and merge at the end.

### Memory consistency (related)
Coherence covers a single location; **consistency models** define the ordering of operations across different locations. x86 has a fairly strong model (TSO); ARM is weaker, so programmers use **memory barriers** and atomics (`volatile` in Java, `std::atomic` in C++).

### Interview questions
**Q: Your multithreaded counter got slower as you added threads. Why?**
Likely false sharing or contention on one cache line. Use per-thread counters padded onto separate cache lines (like Java's `LongAdder`) and sum them when needed.

notes.title: Virtual Memory and the TLB: Hardware View
notes.body:
The hardware side of virtual memory is the MMU, which translates every virtual address using page tables, accelerated by the TLB cache of recent translations.

### The MMU
The **memory management unit** sits between the CPU and the caches/memory. For every access it:
1. Splits the virtual address into a virtual page number (VPN) and an offset.
2. Looks up the VPN in the **TLB**.
3. On a hit, combines the physical frame number with the offset.
4. On a miss, walks the page table (in hardware on x86 and ARM), refills the TLB and retries.
5. If the page isn't present, raises a **page fault** for the OS to handle.
6. Checks permissions (read/write/execute, user/kernel) and raises a protection fault if violated.

### TLB facts
- Small (about 64–1,536 entries), often split into L1 and L2 TLBs.
- Hit rates typically exceed 99% thanks to locality.
- **TLB reach** = entries × page size. **Huge pages** (2 MB or 1 GB) greatly increase reach.
- On a context switch the TLB must be flushed, unless entries are tagged with an **ASID/PCID** (address-space ID).

### Multi-level page walks
x86-64 uses a 4-level (or 5-level) table: PML4 → PDPT → PD → PT. A TLB miss can therefore need 4 memory accesses, which is why **page-walk caches** exist.

### Caches and virtual addresses
- **Physically indexed, physically tagged (PIPT):** translate first; simple but slower.
- **Virtually indexed, physically tagged (VIPT):** look up the cache set and the TLB in parallel. This is common for L1 caches, and is a reason why L1 size is limited to page size × associativity.

### Protection features
- The **NX/XD bit** marks pages non-executable, defending against code injection.
- **User/supervisor bits** keep user code out of kernel memory.
- **ASLR** randomises where code, stack and heap are placed.

### Interview questions
**Q: Why are huge pages good for databases and JVMs with large heaps?**
Each TLB entry covers much more memory, so TLB misses and page-walk costs drop sharply for large, randomly accessed memory.

notes.title: I/O Organization: Polling, Interrupts and DMA
notes.body:
I/O organisation covers how the CPU communicates with devices: how devices are addressed, and how the CPU learns that a device is ready or has finished.

### Addressing devices
- **Memory-mapped I/O:** device registers appear at memory addresses; ordinary load and store instructions access them. Used by ARM and most modern devices.
- **Port-mapped (isolated) I/O:** a separate address space with special instructions (`IN`/`OUT` on x86).

### Three ways to transfer data
| Technique | How it works | CPU cost | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Programmed I/O (polling)** | The CPU loops, checking a status register | High: busy waiting | Very fast devices or very short waits |
| **Interrupt-driven I/O** | The device raises an interrupt when ready; the CPU runs a handler | Moderate: one interrupt per transfer unit | Keyboards, low-rate devices |
| **DMA (direct memory access)** | The DMA controller copies whole blocks between device and memory, then interrupts once | Low: CPU free during the transfer | Disks, network cards, GPUs |

### How DMA works
1. The CPU programs the DMA controller with a source, destination, byte count and direction.
2. The DMA controller takes control of the bus and transfers the data. It may **cycle-steal**: briefly delay the CPU's own memory accesses.
3. When done, it raises **one** interrupt.

### Interrupt handling details
- **Vectored interrupts:** the device supplies a vector number, which selects its handler.
- **Priority and masking:** higher-priority interrupts can preempt lower ones, and interrupts can be disabled during critical code.
- **Top half / bottom half:** the handler does minimal work immediately and defers the rest (softirqs, tasklets) to keep interrupt latency low.

### Modern twists
- **Interrupt coalescing / NAPI:** under heavy network load, switch from interrupts to polling to avoid an "interrupt storm".
- **IOMMU:** translates and restricts device DMA addresses, for security and virtualisation.
- **NVMe:** many parallel submission and completion queues for SSDs.

### Interview questions
**Q: When is polling better than interrupts?**
When events are very frequent or must be handled with very low latency (high-speed networking, NVMe at high queue depth). The overhead of each interrupt (context switch, cache pollution) then exceeds the cost of spinning.

notes.title: Parallelism: Multicore, SIMD and Amdahl's Law
notes.body:
Modern performance comes from parallelism at many levels: inside one instruction (SIMD), across instructions (pipelining, superscalar), across threads (multicore) and across machines.

### Flynn's taxonomy
| Class | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| SISD | Single instruction, single data | Classic single-core CPU |
| SIMD | One instruction on many data elements | AVX, NEON, GPU warps |
| MISD | Multiple instructions on the same data | Rare (fault-tolerant systems) |
| MIMD | Independent instructions on independent data | Multicore CPUs, clusters |

### Levels of parallelism
- **Instruction-level (ILP):** pipelining, superscalar and out-of-order execution.
- **Data-level (DLP):** SIMD vector units process, for example, 8 floats per AVX instruction; GPUs run thousands of threads.
- **Thread-level (TLP):** multicore CPUs and **SMT / Hyper-Threading** (two hardware threads sharing one core's execution units).

### Amdahl's law
If a fraction **p** of a program can be parallelised over **N** processors:
**Speedup = 1 / ((1 − p) + p / N)**

Example: p = 0.9 and N = 8 gives a speedup of 1 / (0.1 + 0.1125) ≈ **4.7×**. Even with infinitely many cores, the maximum is 1 / 0.1 = **10×**. The serial part dominates.

### Gustafson's law
A more optimistic view: as you get more cores you usually solve **bigger problems**, so the parallel part grows. Scaled speedup = N − (1 − p)(N − 1).

### Why parallel code is hard
- Synchronisation overhead and lock contention.
- Load imbalance between threads.
- Cache coherence traffic and false sharing.
- Memory bandwidth limits (the "memory wall").

### Multicore memory organisation
- **UMA:** all cores see uniform memory latency.
- **NUMA:** each socket has local memory; remote access is slower. NUMA-aware allocation and thread pinning matter on servers.

### Interview questions
**Q: Your code is 95% parallel. What's the best speedup on 100 cores?**
1 / (0.05 + 0.95 / 100) = 1 / 0.0595 ≈ **16.8×**. The 5% serial part caps the overall gain.

notes.title: Endianness, Alignment and Data Layout
notes.body:
Endianness is the byte order of multi-byte values in memory, and alignment is placing data at addresses that are multiples of its size; both affect correctness and speed of low-level code.

### Endianness
Storing the 32-bit value `0x12345678` at address 100:
| Address | 100 | 101 | 102 | 103 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Big-endian** | 12 | 34 | 56 | 78 |
| **Little-endian** | 78 | 56 | 34 | 12 |

- **Little-endian:** x86, most ARM configurations, RISC-V.
- **Big-endian:** network byte order (TCP/IP headers), some older architectures.
- Convert with `htonl`/`ntohl` (host-to-network and back) when writing binary protocols or files.

**Check the endianness in C:**
```c
uint32_t x = 1;
int little = *(uint8_t *)&x == 1;
```

### Alignment
A 4-byte `int` is **aligned** if its address is a multiple of 4. Unaligned accesses may span two cache lines (slower), and on some architectures they raise an error.

### Struct padding
Compilers insert padding so each field is aligned:
```c
struct A { char c; int i; char d; };   // 1 + 3 pad + 4 + 1 + 3 pad = 12 bytes
struct B { int i; char c; char d; };   // 4 + 1 + 1 + 2 pad = 8 bytes
```
**Ordering fields from largest to smallest** reduces padding. `#pragma pack` and `__attribute__((packed))` remove padding at the cost of slower, unaligned access.

### Data-oriented layout
- **Array of structs (AoS):** `particles[i].x, .y, .z`. Natural to write.
- **Struct of arrays (SoA):** `xs[i], ys[i], zs[i]`. Better cache use and SIMD when you process one field across many items.

### Interview questions
**Q: Why might `sizeof(struct)` be larger than the sum of its fields?**
Because of padding added for alignment, both between fields and at the end, so that elements in an array of that struct stay aligned.
